<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{definition:EIGS}
A \emph{random edge iterated graph system} (random EIGS) is specified by the following data and iteration.
{\small
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.,leftmargin=*,topsep=3pt,itemsep=1pt,parsep=0pt]
\item \textbf{Initial graph.} A finite directed graph $\Xi^0$ with edge colours in $[K]:=\{1,\ldots,K\}$; parallel edges are allowed. For a single initial edge, write its endpoints as $\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-$.
\item \textbf{Rule laws.} For each colour, a fixed probability law on finitely many finite directed rule graphs, with the same colour set and two ordered distinct \emph{planting vertices}.
\item \textbf{Substitution.} Replace each edge $(a,b)$ by a fresh rule sampled according to its colour, identifying the planting vertices with $a,b$ and making no further identifications. Samples are independent across edges, with fresh randomness at each step.
\item \textbf{Iteration.} Simultaneous substitution produces the \emph{substitution networks} $\Xi^0,\Xi^1,\ldots$. The EIGS is \emph{deterministic} if every rule law is concentrated on one graph.
\end{enumerate}}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:standing}
A \textbf{classical EIGS hierarchical lattice} is generated from a single directed edge by a deterministic single-colour EIGS with a finite, connected, simple rule graph $R=(V(R),E(R);\beta^+,\beta^-)$.
Connectivity, distances and percolation refer to its underlying undirected graph.
{\small
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.,leftmargin=*,topsep=3pt,itemsep=1pt,parsep=0pt]
\item \textbf{Canonicality.} Every edge lies on a simple path between $\beta^+$ and $\beta^-$.
\item \textbf{Geometric bounds.} We require $\ell:=d_R(\beta^+,\beta^-)\ge2$ and $\operatorname{mincut}_R(\beta^+,\beta^-)\ge2$, where $\operatorname{mincut}_R(\beta^+,\beta^-)$ is the minimum size of a terminal-separating edge cut.
\item \textbf{Terminal symmetry.} The underlying undirected graph admits an involutive automorphism exchanging $\beta^+$ and $\beta^-$.
\end{enumerate}}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- restated-1: body_md -->
{prop:chemical-minkowski-dimension}
Almost surely,
\[
\dim_{\mathrm B}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})=\frac{\log\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})} {\log\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}}.
\]
<!-- end restated-1 -->
<!-- restated-2: body_md -->
{thm:resistance-exponent}
For every classical EIGS hierarchical lattice, there is a deterministic $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}>1$ such that, almost surely,
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_n}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)}{n}
=\log\lambda_{\mathfrak C}.
\]
<!-- end restated-2 -->
<!-- restated-3: body_md -->
{thm:heat-kernels}
Almost surely, for $\mu$-almost every $x\in \mathfrak C$,
\[
 \dim_{\mathrm S}^{(\mathrm N)}(\mathfrak C:x)
 =
 \frac{2\dim_{\mathrm B}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})}{\dim_{\mathrm B}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})+\dim_{\mathrm R}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})}.
\]
<!-- end restated-3 -->
<!-- restated-4: body_md -->
{thm:ao-region}
For every classical EIGS rule, if
\[
 (\dim_{\mathrm B}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}}),\dim_{\mathrm R}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}}))
 \notin (\frac{4}{3},2)\times(\frac{2}{3},1),
\]
then the typical spectral dimension of the natural limiting diffusion on its critical cluster satisfies
\[
 \dim_{\mathrm S}^{(\mathrm N)}(\mathfrak C)\neq\frac{4}{3}.
\]
<!-- end restated-4 -->
<!-- restated-5: body_md -->
{thm:spectral-density}
The typical spectral dimensions $\dim_{\mathrm S}^{(\mathrm N)}(\mathfrak C)$ of the natural limiting diffusions on critical percolation clusters of classical EIGS hierarchical lattices are dense in $(1,2)$.
<!-- end restated-5 -->
<!-- restated-6: body_md -->
{conj:ao-global}
For every classical EIGS hierarchical lattice at its own critical point, the typical spectral dimension of the natural limiting diffusion on the full terminal-connected cluster satisfies
\[
\dim_{\mathrm S}^{(\mathrm N)}(\mathfrak C) \neq \frac{4}{3}.
\]
That is, the Alexander-Orbach conjecture does not hold on classical EIGS hierarchical lattices.
<!-- end restated-6 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:critical-cluster}
As in \cite[Section~2.1]{NeroliIGSII2026}, let $\mathfrak C_n$ be the full terminal-connected cluster in $\Xi^n$, conditioned on crossing, including all dangling branches.
Its chemical distance $d_{\mathfrak C_n}$ is the intrinsic graph distance along open edges.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:chemical-elementary-bounds}
For every $n\ge0$ and every terminal-connected configuration,
\[
 \ell^n\le d_{\mathfrak C_n}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\le L^n.
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
At depth zero the terminal distance is one.
Coarsening a terminal path at depth $n+1$ gives a crossing of the rule graph and hence contains a simple terminal path of at least $\ell$ edges.
Each corresponding depth-$n$ cell must be crossed, so induction gives the lower bound.
Conversely, choose a simple open terminal path in the coarse rule, which has at most $L$ edges, and cross each of its cells along a shortest open path.
Induction bounds the resulting path length by $L^{n+1}$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:chemical-recursion}
Let $\mathcal Q_c$ be the Bernoulli-$p_c$ rule law conditioned on crossing, and let $H$ be the union of its open edges lying on simple terminal paths.
For nonnegative edge lengths $x$, define the shortest-path functional
\[
 F_H^{\mathrm{ch}}(x):=\min_P\sum_{e\in P}x_e,
\]
where $P$ ranges over the simple terminal paths of $H$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:chemical-path-functional}
The function $F_H^{\mathrm{ch}}$ is increasing, concave, positively homogeneous and superadditive, and satisfies
\[
 |F_H^{\mathrm{ch}}(x)-F_H^{\mathrm{ch}}(y)|\le\sum_e|x_e-y_e|.
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Each path cost is linear with nonnegative coefficients, so its minimum is increasing, concave and positively homogeneous.
For every path, its cost at $x+y$ is at least $F_H^{\mathrm{ch}}(x)+F_H^{\mathrm{ch}}(y)$, which proves superadditivity.
Evaluating the cost at $x$ along a minimising path for $y$, and then exchanging $x$ and $y$, gives the stated bound.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:chemical-field}
There are a deterministic $\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}\in[\ell,L]$ and a strictly positive mean-one field $(X_u^{\mathrm{ch}})$, measurable with respect to the innovation tree, such that almost surely at every connected address,
\[
 F_{H_u}^{\mathrm{ch}}(X_{ui}^{\mathrm{ch}})=\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}X_u^{\mathrm{ch}}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lem:chemical-moments} constructs the mean-one eigenlaw and proves its moment bounds. Lemma~\ref{lem:chemical-compactness} realises it on the original innovation tree. The recursion holds at each address by that construction, and a countable intersection gives the simultaneous assertion. The lower bound $\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}\ge\ell$ follows from the first-moment estimate in Lemma~\ref{lem:chemical-compactness}; the selected-path bound in Lemma~\ref{lem:chemical-moments} gives $\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}\le L$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:chemical-field-integrability}
The marginal law of the field in Theorem~\ref{thm:chemical-field} has every positive and negative moment and every finite positive exponential moment.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The field constructed in Lemma~\ref{lem:chemical-compactness} has the marginal law of Lemma~\ref{lem:chemical-moments}, where these integrability properties are proved.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:chemical-scalar}
For the field of Theorem~\ref{thm:chemical-field}, there is a deterministic $c_{\mathrm{ch}}\ge1$ such that
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{u,n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)=
 c_{\mathrm{ch}}X_u^{\mathrm{ch}}
 \quad\text{almost surely and in every finite positive }L^p
\]
simultaneously at every connected address.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Lemmas~\ref{lem:chemical-moments}--\ref{lem:chemical-endpoint}, proved in Appendix~\ref{app:chemical}, apply to the field of Theorem~\ref{thm:chemical-field} and give a deterministic $c\ge1$ and a subsequence along which $\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)$ converges to $cX^{\mathrm{ch}}$ in $L^2$.
The remaining step is to pass from that subsequence to every depth.
Select $n_j$ with $\displaystyle\lim_{j\to\infty}\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-{n_j}}d_{\mathfrak C_{n_j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)=cX^{\mathrm{ch}}$ in $L^2$.
Fix $0<\varepsilon<c$ and choose $\theta>0$ so that $C_R\mathbb E e^{-\theta\varepsilon X^{\mathrm{ch}}}<1$.
Both $e^{\theta(\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-{n_j}}d_{\mathfrak C_{n_j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)-(c+\varepsilon)X^{\mathrm{ch}})}$ and $e^{\theta((c-\varepsilon)X^{\mathrm{ch}}-\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-{n_j}}d_{\mathfrak C_{n_j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr))}$ converge in probability to $e^{-\theta\varepsilon X^{\mathrm{ch}}}$.
Uniform positive exponential moments make them uniformly integrable.
Choose one fixed $j$ for which both signed conditions in Lemma~\ref{lem:chemical-paths} hold.

Above this block, the pairs $(\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-{n_j}}d_{\mathfrak C_{n_j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr),X^{\mathrm{ch}})$ are independent across the exposed leaves and retain their within-pair coupling.
Outside a summable sequence of exceptions, every terminal path satisfies both signed comparisons.
Taking minima gives $(c-\varepsilon)X^{\mathrm{ch}}\le \bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-{n+n_j}}d_{\mathfrak C_{n+n_j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\le(c+\varepsilon)X^{\mathrm{ch}}$ for every sufficiently large $n$.
This fixed shift covers the whole eventual sequence.
A countable sequence $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives almost-sure convergence.
Uniform moments give every finite positive $L^p$ convergence and convergence of means.
Set $c_{\mathrm{ch}}:=c$.
A countable address intersection proves the field assertion.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:chemical-scales}
If all simple terminal paths of the rule have length $\ell$, induction gives $d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)=\ell^n$ on every crossing cluster; hence $\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}=\ell$ and $X^{\mathrm{ch}}=1$.
For the standard diamond, this gives $\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}=2$.

Strict inequality already occurs for a five-cycle with terminal paths of lengths two and three.
Its terminal exchange fixes the middle vertex of the shorter path and interchanges the two internal vertices of the longer path, so it is a classical rule.
Here $\ell=2$ and $\varphi_R(p)=p^2+p^3-p^5$; the interior critical point satisfies $p_c^3+p_c^2=1$.
Conditioned on a crossing, the two coarse branches are open with probabilities $p_c$ and $p_c^2$.
For independent copies of $d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)$, convexity gives
$\mathbb E(d_{\mathfrak C_{n,1}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)+\cdots+d_{\mathfrak C_{n,j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-))^{-3}\le j^{-3}\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)^{-3}$.
The inverse cube of the minimum over open branches is at most the sum of their inverse cubes, so
\[
 \mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n+1}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)^{-3}\le\left(\frac{p_c}{8}+\frac{p_c^2}{27}\right)\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)^{-3}.
\]
Iteration and Markov's inequality show that, for every
$c<(p_c/8+p_c^2/27)^{-1/3}$, the probabilities $\mathbb P(d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\le c^n)$ are summable.
Consequently
\[
 \ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}\ge
 \left(\frac{p_c}{8}+\frac{p_c^2}{27}\right)^{-1/3}\approx2.0536>2.
\]
The strict inequality also follows without numerical approximation:
$p_c<4/5$ gives $p_c/8+p_c^2/27<167/1350<1/8$.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:retained-states}
We retain the states $c,b,u,0$ and the inherited endpoint markings of \cite[Definition~2.7 and Theorem~2.8]{NeroliIGSII2026}.
The state $c$ retains the crossing component, $b$ retains both terminal components of a noncrossing cell, $u$ retains one specified terminal component of a noncrossing cell, and $0$ retains nothing.
A cell of state $u$ carries its inherited active terminal as a mark; terminal symmetry identifies the two choices in law.
For a child edge, assign $c$ when it is open and both endpoints are active, $b$ when it is closed and both endpoints are active, $u$ when exactly one endpoint is active, and $0$ otherwise.
At depth zero the retained objects are an open edge, two isolated terminals, one marked terminal, or the empty set, according to their state.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:population-limit}
Almost surely,
\[
 \lim_{k\to\infty}\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^{-k}\mathbf Z_k=W_c\mathbf v,
 \qquad W_c>0.
\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The finite-type Kesten--Stigum theorem gives almost-sure population convergence because $\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C}$ is primitive and the offspring are bounded \cite{KurtzLyonsPemantlePeres1997}.
The $L^2$ identification in \cite[proof of Lemma~3.3]{NeroliIGSII2026} identifies its scalar limit with $W_c$ under the stated Perron normalisation.
The same lemma and its proof give a density for the nonnegative mass limit, hence $W_c>0$ almost surely.
Applying the argument at each fixed descendant and taking a countable intersection gives the corresponding limits simultaneously throughout the tree.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:vertex-mass-limit}
Almost surely,
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^{-n}|V(\mathfrak C_n)|=W_c.
\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Fix a live root state $\sigma$ and use the exact birth recursion in \cite[proof of Lemma~3.2]{NeroliIGSII2026}.
The total reward in generation $k$, after subtraction of its conditional mean, has variance at most $C\mathbb E|\mathbf Z_k|=O(\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^k)$.
Chebyshev's inequality and Borel--Cantelli show that division by $\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^k$ makes this centred reward tend to zero almost surely.
Its conditional mean is a fixed linear function of $\mathbf Z_k$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:population-limit} and summation of the resulting geometric series therefore give almost-sure convergence of the normalised accumulated rewards.
The limit equals $W_\sigma$ by the $L^2$ convergence already proved in \cite[proof of Lemma~3.3]{NeroliIGSII2026}; including the outer terminals changes the count by at most two.
For the root, $\sigma=c$ gives the asserted limit.
The same argument at every fixed live descendant gives the limit $W_{T_u}^{(u)}$ on one common event of probability one.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:mass-perron}
Every fixed retained-component cylinder has a compatible limiting normalised vertex mass, with positive mass for connected cylinders.
The two sides of $b$ use their original joint law.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:vertex-mass-limit} at every fixed descendant address.
For one side of $b$, retain its raw innovations and use the $u$ root mask with that side's active-terminal mark.
This gives precisely that component on the existing coupling, with the correct marginal one-arm law.
Its counting limit exists, and the two masked limits sum to the $b$ limit.
Assign shared frontier vertices by any fixed convention.
Different conventions affect finitely many vertices, whose normalised mass tends to zero.
A component at address $u$ therefore has limiting mass $\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^{-|u|}$ times its masked martingale limit divided by the positive root limit.
Finite-depth decomposition identities pass to these ratios and give compatibility.
Connected-cylinder positivity follows from the strict positivity in Lemma~\ref{lem:population-limit}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:full-ghp}
There is a random compact two-marked metric--measure space
\[
 (\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}},\mu,\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)
\]
with full-support measure such that
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}(\mathfrak C_n,(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_n},\frac{1}{|V(\mathfrak C_n)|}\sum_{x\in V(\mathfrak C_n)}\delta_x,\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)
 =(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}},\mu,\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)
\]
almost surely along the whole sequence in two-marked Gromov--Hausdorff--Prokhorov topology.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let $V_k$ contain the retained vertices born by generation $k$.
For $n\ge k$, replace each connected generation-$k$ cell by an edge of length $d_{\mathfrak C_{u,n-k}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)$.
Other frontier states supply no through-edge.
Connected dangling branches remain.
Compressing microscopic paths and removing one-attachment excursions, and conversely expanding skeleton edges along terminal geodesics, prove that this weighted distance is exactly the restriction of $d_{\mathfrak C_n}$ to $V_k$.

Each scaled skeleton edge tends to the positive value $c_{\mathrm{ch}}(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-k}X_u^{\mathrm{ch}}$.
Finite shortest-path matrices are continuous in their edge lengths.
The scalar recursion makes the limiting metrics compatible on successive $V_k$.
Every fixed skeleton has positive distances between distinct vertices.
We obtain a metric $d_{\mathrm{ch}}$ on $V_*=\bigcup_kV_k$.
Component anchors form $\Gamma_k$-nets both for later approximants and for $V_*$.
Thus its completion $\mathfrak C$ is compact.
Match skeleton labels and project the remaining points to anchors.
For fixed $k$ the finite distance errors vanish with $n$, and the projection errors are at most $\Gamma_k$.
Letting $n\to\infty$ and then $k\to\infty$ proves the marked metric convergence.

Project each component's mass to its planted anchor.
Lemma~\ref{lem:mass-perron} gives convergence of these finitely many masses.
The allocation error at old junction vertices vanishes.
Compatibility and the vanishing mesh make the limiting atomic measures a Cauchy family on $\mathfrak C$, defining $\mu$.
The same transports bound the Prokhorov error by the mesh and the vanishing allocation error.
This proves the asserted measured convergence.

Every skeleton vertex is incident to a connected frontier cell.
This follows from its active coarse connection at birth and the connected replacements of incident edges thereafter.
It has arbitrarily fine connected cylinders with positive limiting mass and vanishing diameter.
Every neighbourhood of each skeleton vertex therefore has positive mass.
Density proves full support.
Theorem~\ref{thm:chemical-scalar} also identifies the terminal distance as $d_{\mathrm{ch}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)=c_{\mathrm{ch}}X_\varnothing^{\mathrm{ch}}>0$.

Measurability follows from convergence of the measurable finite marked spaces.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:cell-localisation}
The intrinsic retained components embed continuously in $\mathfrak C$, with distinct components at the same generation intersecting only at shared planted vertices.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The intrinsic skeleton metric is positive and its completion compact by the component mesh.
Inclusion is $1$-Lipschitz.
For skeleton points in one component, first exit and last entrance give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cell-route}
 d_{\mathrm{ch}}(x,y)=
 \min\left\{d_A(x,y),
 \min_{a,b\in\partial A}
 [d_A(x,a)+d_{\mathrm{ch}}(a,b)+d_A(b,y)]\right\}.
\end{equation}
Conversely these costs are approached by concatenating the indicated routes.
The equality passes from finite approximants to skeleton limits and then, by continuity and finiteness of the boundary, to completions.
If two distinct intrinsic points had the same image, this formula would force them to be distinct planted boundary points with the same image.
Their positive finite-skeleton distance excludes this.
The analogous first-exit calculation between distinct components shows that intersections are only planted ones.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:cell-separation}
For distinct retained components $A,B$ at the same generation and $x\in A$, $y\in B$,
\[
 d_{\mathrm{ch}}(x,y)\ge d_A(x,\partial A)+d_B(y,\partial B).
\]
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
For skeleton points, any route from $x$ to $y$ must leave $A$ through $\partial A$ and enter $B$ through $\partial B$.
Its initial and final segments therefore have total length at least the right-hand side.
This bound passes from finite approximants to the skeleton limit, and then to the intrinsic completions by continuity.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:cell-scaling-law}
Conditional on the raw innovation pairs $(\xi_u^c,\xi_u^N)$ with $|u|<k$, the intrinsic completions of distinct generation-$k$ state-$c$ cells are independent, each with law $(\mathfrak C,(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-k}d_{\mathrm{ch}})$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The generation-$k$ types are determined by the conditioned innovations.
The descendant innovation trees at distinct generation-$k$ addresses use disjoint coordinates and are conditionally independent.
Each state-$c$ intrinsic completion depends only on its descendant tree, and its edge lengths carry the deterministic factor $(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-k}$, giving the scaled root law.
The two sides of a state-$b$ cell use the same noncrossing innovation and retain their joint law.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:chemical-dimension}
For a compact metric space, let $\mathcal N(r)$ be the minimum number of radius-$r$ balls needed to cover it.
Its Minkowski dimension is the common value of the lower and upper limits of $\log\mathcal N(r)/\log(1/r)$ as $r$ tends to zero, when these agree.
For $(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})$ we call this the chemical Minkowski dimension.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:chemical-minkowski-dimension}
Almost surely,
\[
\dim_{\mathrm B}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})=\frac{\log\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})} {\log\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The all-order chemical component-diameter bounds and a frontier union bound give
$\max_{A\in\mathcal A_k}\operatorname{diam}_{d_{\mathrm{ch}}}(A)
 \le C_{\omega,\varepsilon}(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-k}e^{\varepsilon k}$.
There are $O_\omega(\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^k)$ components and they cover $\mathfrak C$.
For $0<\varepsilon<\log\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}$, interpolation gives upper Minkowski dimension at most
$\log\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})/(\log\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}-\varepsilon)$.
Let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$.

Choose an interior vertex $z$ on a first-generation crossing path in a fresh connected cell.
Since $\ell\ge2$, this vertex differs from both planted terminals, and the limiting first-skeleton edge lengths are positive.
Thus its intrinsic distance $\Delta$ to the planted boundary is strictly positive.
Choose deterministic $r_0>0$ with $\mathbb P_c(\Delta\ge r_0)>0$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:cell-scaling-law}, the connected population limit and Chernoff bounds give at least $c_\omega\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^k$ generation-$k$ connected cells whose corresponding vertices have intrinsic boundary distance at least $r_0(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-k}$, eventually.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:cell-separation}, their selected points are pairwise separated by at least $r_0(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-k}$ in the full-cluster chemical metric.
A ball of one third that radius contains at most one selected point.
Thus $\mathcal N(r_0(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-k}/3)\ge c_\omega\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^k$.
Interpolation gives the lower Minkowski dimension.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:electrical-eigenlaw}
There are $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}\in[\varphi_R'(p_c),\mathbb E|P(H)|]$ and a strictly positive mean-one variable $X$ with $\mathbb E(X^p+X^{-p})<\infty$ for every $p>0$, such that $F_H(X_e)$ has the law of $\lambda_{\mathfrak C} X$ for independent child copies, independent of $H$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Thomson's principle writes $F_H(x)$ as the infimum of $\sum_ex_eI_e^2$ over unit terminal flows.
Thus it is increasing, concave, positively homogeneous and superadditive.
The unit electrical current satisfies $|I_e|\le1$: orient nonzero currents along decreasing potential and decompose this acyclic flow into terminal path flows with total weight one.
An optimal trial current therefore gives $|F_H(x)-F_H(y)|\le\sum_e|x_e-y_e|$, including the continuous extension to nonnegative resistances.


Every edge lying on all terminal paths carries unit current.
Their expected number is $\varphi_R'(p_c)$ by \textcolor{black}{\cite[proof of Lemma~2.16]{NeroliIGSII2026}}.
The chosen path supplies an upper trial flow.
For independent nonnegative mean-one inputs $Y_e$, therefore, $\varphi_R'(p_c)\le\mathbb E F_H(Y_e)\le \mathbb E|P(H)|$.


Normalise the output by its mean and denote the resulting law map by $\widehat T$.
The same selected-path multinomial argument as in Lemma~\ref{lem:chemical-moments} gives
\[
 \int_0^\infty x^p\,(\widehat T\nu)(dx)\le(\mathbb E|P(H)|/\varphi_R'(p_c)^p)\left(\int_0^\infty x^p\,\nu(dx)\right)
                   +A_p\left(\int_0^\infty x^p\,\nu(dx)\right)^{(p-2)/(p-1)}.
\]
For all sufficiently large integers $p$, choose invariant bounds $K_p\ge1$.
The mean-one laws satisfying all these bounds form a nonempty convex weakly compact set.
Higher moments preserve the mean under limits, the constraints are closed, and the electrical Lipschitz estimate makes $\widehat T$ continuous.
Schauder's theorem yields an eigenlaw with every positive moment and $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}\in[\varphi_R'(p_c),\mathbb E|P(H)|]$.


In a network of at most $m$ edges, effective resistance at most $a>0$ forces the edges of resistance at most $ma$ to contain a terminal path.
Otherwise the vertices reachable through such edges determine a terminal cut with conductance strictly less than $1/a$, contradicting the bound on effective conductance.


Independent marking of coarse core edges with probability $u$ gives crossing probability $g(u)$.
This follows by thinning the original Bernoulli-$p_c$ configuration; crossing of the thinned configuration already implies the conditioning event.
Consequently $z=\mathbb P(X=0)$ obeys $z=g(z)$.
The mean and the inequality $g(u)<u$ for $0<u<1$ give $z=0$.
For $F(t):=\mathbb P(X\le t)$ the small-edge observation gives $F(t)\le g(F(m\lambda_{\mathfrak C} t))$.
Starting with $F(t_0)<1$ and iterating yields
$F(t_0(m\lambda_{\mathfrak C})^{-k})\le\exp(-c\ell^k)$ after finitely many terms.
Integration proves every inverse moment.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:electrical-field}
The eigenlaw has a stationary realisation $(X_u)$ measurable with respect to the original innovation tree.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Independent eigenlaw values on a finite boundary and upward recursion give consistent finite-dimensional distributions.
Their extension satisfies $F_{H_u}(X_{ue})=\lambda_{\mathfrak C} X_u$, with independent descendant subtrees.
For a fixed outer network $G$ with independent resistances $Y_i$, write $Z=F_G(Y)$.
Replacing $Y_i$ by an independent $Y_i'$ gives
$(F_G(Y^{(i)})-F_G(Y))_+\le I_i(Y)^2Y_i'$ by a trial current.
One-sided Efron--Stein gives
$\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid G)\le\mathbb E Y^2\,\mathbb E[\sum_iI_i(Y)^4\mid G]$.
Since $|I_i|\le1$ and $\sum_iY_iI_i^2=Z$, one has $\sum_iI_i^4\le Z\max_iY_i^{-1}$.
For at most $m^k$ edges and $p\ge2$,
\[
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid G)\le\mathbb E Y^2\,\|Z\|_2m^{k/p}\|Y^{-1}\|_p.
\]
With stationary leaves the output is $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^kX$.
Choosing $p$ with $m^{1/p}/\lambda_{\mathfrak C}<1$ gives
$\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(X_\varnothing\mid\mathcal F_k)\le C(m^{1/p}/\lambda_{\mathfrak C})^k$.
Thus $X_\varnothing$ is measurable with respect to the complete innovation tree.
A countable intersection gives this at every address.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:electrical-sandwich}
\[
 \mathbb E[X_\varnothing\mid\mathcal F_n]\le \bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\le\frac{(\mathbb E X_\varnothing^{-1})}{\mathbb E[X_\varnothing^{-1}\mid\mathcal F_n]}\le(\mathbb E X_\varnothing^{-1}) \mathbb E[X_\varnothing\mid\mathcal F_n].
\]
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Concavity in resistances gives $\mathbb E[X_\varnothing\mid\mathcal F_n]\le \bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)$.
The effective conductance $c\mapsto F_{\mathcal H_n}(c^{-1})^{-1}$ is concave by the Dirichlet principle.
Applying it to the stationary boundary conductances gives $\mathbb E[X_\varnothing^{-1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\le(\mathbb E X_\varnothing^{-1})/\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)$.
Conditional Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\mathbb E[X_\varnothing\mid\mathcal F_n]\mathbb E[X_\varnothing^{-1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\ge1$.
This proves the sandwich.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:electrical-uniform-moments}
For every $p>0$, $\sup_n\mathbb E(\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)^p+\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)^{-p})<\infty$ and $\mathbb E(\sup_n\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr))^p<\infty$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The bounds of Lemma~\ref{lem:electrical-sandwich} give the required comparison with conditional martingales.
The two conditional martingales converge to $X_\varnothing$ and $X_\varnothing^{-1}$.
The pathwise and mean assertions follow.
Conditional Jensen gives
$\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)^{-p}\le \mathbb E[X_\varnothing\mid\mathcal F_n]^{-p}\le\mathbb E[X_\varnothing^{-p}\mid\mathcal F_n]$.
For positive moments use $\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\le(\mathbb E X_\varnothing^{-1}) \mathbb E[X_\varnothing\mid\mathcal F_n]$.
Doob's inequality at an order larger than $\max\{1,p\}$ gives the moment of $\sup_n\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:resistance-exponent}
There is a deterministic $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}>1$ such that
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)}{n}
 =\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb E\log\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)}{n}
 =\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log\mathbb E\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)}{n}
 =\log\lambda_{\mathfrak C},
\]
where the first limit holds almost surely.
The conclusions hold at every fixed connected address, and $\varphi_R'(p_c)\le\lambda_{\mathfrak C}\le \mathbb E|P(H)|$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Take the value of $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:electrical-eigenlaw}.
The sandwich bounds $\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)$ eventually between strictly positive finite random constants.
Hence
\[
 \displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\log \bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)=0\textcolor{black}{.}
\]


The bounds $1\le\mathbb E \bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\le(\mathbb E X_\varnothing^{-1})$ and
$\sup_n\mathbb E|\log \bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)|<\infty$, the latter following from $|\log x|\le x+x^{-1}$, prove the first-moment and mean-log limits separately.
Take the countable intersection over connected addresses.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:resistance-moment-exponents}
For every fixed $t\in\mathbb R$,
$\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n}\log\mathbb E\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)^t
=t\log\lambda_{\mathfrak C}$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The uniform moment bounds in Lemma~\ref{lem:electrical-uniform-moments} apply.
For $t\ne0$, uniform positive and inverse moments give
$C_{-t}^{-1}\le\mathbb E \bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)^t\le C_t$, since
\[
\mathbb E \bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)^t\,\mathbb E \bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)^{-t}\ge1.
\]
Their logarithms divided by $n$ vanish.
The case $t=0$ is immediate.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:electrical-compactness}
The sequence $\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)$ is relatively compact in the original $L^2$ space.
Its omega-limit set contains $cX_\varnothing$ for a deterministic $c\in[1,(\mathbb E X_\varnothing^{-1})]$.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
For $n\ge k$, expose $\mathcal F_k$ and place independent copies of $\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-{n-k}}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n-k}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)$ at its leaves.
The output is $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^k\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)$.
Uniform positive and inverse moments in the electrical variance calculation yield
$\sup_{n\ge k}\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\mid\mathcal F_k)\le C\theta^k$ for some $\theta<1$.
For $n<k$ the variance is zero.
The bounded conditional expectations lie in a finite-dimensional space because $\mathcal F_k$ has finitely many atoms.
Their uniform approximation proves relative compactness.


Define $Tf:=\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-1}F_H(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$ on functions of the innovation tree.
It is $L^2$-continuous and $\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)=T^n1$.
The nonempty compact omega-limit set $\mathcal K$ satisfies $T\mathcal K=\mathcal K$.
Every $h\in\mathcal K$ obeys $X_\varnothing\le h\le(\mathbb E X_\varnothing^{-1}) X_\varnothing$ by further almost-sure subsequences.
Put $c:=\sup_{h\in\mathcal K}\operatorname{ess\,sup}(h/X_\varnothing)$.


If $cX_\varnothing\notin\mathcal K$, the nonnegative deficits $cX_\varnothing-h$ have means bounded away from zero and uniformly bounded second moments.
Paley--Zygmund gives $Q(t_0)\le1-\varepsilon$ for some $t_0,\varepsilon>0$, where $Q(t)=\sup_h\mathbb P((cX_\varnothing-h)\le t)$.
Superadditivity gives $(cX_\varnothing-Th)\ge T(cX_\varnothing-h)$.
Predecessors and the electrical small-edge estimate yield $Q(t)\le g(Q(m\lambda_{\mathfrak C} t))$.
Its iteration gives a finite constant $M$ such that $\sup_h\mathbb E (cX_\varnothing-h)^{-1}\le M$.


For fixed $h$, choose deterministic predecessors $h_{-n}$ with $T^nh_{-n}=h$.
Repeated superadditivity gives $(cX_\varnothing-h)\ge T^n(cX_\varnothing-h_{-n})$.
The leaf deficits are independent conditional on $\mathcal F_n$, with reciprocal mean at most $M$.
Conductance concavity gives
\[
 \mathbb E[(T^n(cX_\varnothing-h_{-n}))^{-1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\le M/\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr).
\]
Conditional Jensen therefore implies
$\mathbb E[(cX_\varnothing-h)\mid\mathcal F_n]\ge \bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)/M\ge \mathbb E[X_\varnothing\mid\mathcal F_n]/M$.
Martingale convergence gives $(cX_\varnothing-h)\ge X_\varnothing/M$ almost surely.
Thus every $h$ has essential ratio at most $c-1/M$, contradicting the definition of $c$.
The same deterministic $M$ works for all $h$; no uncountable common null set is needed for the essential-supremum conclusion.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:electrical-comparison}
Let a finite connected two-terminal graph $G$ carry independent identically distributed pairs of positive edge resistances $(U_e,V_e)$.
Then
\[
 \mathbb E(F_G(U)-F_G(V))_+
 \le \varepsilon(U,V)\mathbb E F_G(V).
\]
The reversed bound holds after exchanging $U,V$.
The coefficient does not depend on the graph.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Hold all other resistances fixed and impose unit terminal current.
For a bridge, the current is constant as its resistance varies.
For a nonbridge, deleting the edge leaves a connected network, and the Thevenin formula gives $I_e(r)=A_e/(r+B_e)$ with $B_e\ge0$.
Thus, for $\vartheta_e(r)=I_e(r)^2$,
\[
 \min\{1,r^{-2}\}\vartheta_e(1)
 \le\vartheta_e(r)\le
 \max\{1,r^{-2}\}\vartheta_e(1).
\]
This also covers constant bridge currents and zero currents.


The optimal $V$ current is a trial flow for $U$, so
$(F_G(U)-F_G(V))_+\le\sum_e(U_e-V_e)_+\vartheta_e(V_e)$.
Conditioning on the other pairs bounds the expected summand above by
$\vartheta_e(1)\mathbb E[(U-V)_+\max\{1,V^{-2}\}]$.
The expected $V_e\vartheta_e(V_e)$ is at least
$\vartheta_e(1)\mathbb E\min\{V,V^{-1}\}$.
Eliminate $\vartheta_e(1)$ and sum, using $\sum_eV_eI_e(V)^2=F_G(V)$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:electrical-amplitudes}
There is a deterministic $c_{\mathrm R}>0$ such that
$\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{u,n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)=c_{\mathrm R}X_u$ almost surely at every connected address and in every finite positive $L^p$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The compactness and comparison estimates are Lemmas~\ref{lem:electrical-compactness} and~\ref{lem:electrical-comparison}.
Choose a deterministic subsequence $j_r$ with $\displaystyle\lim_{r\to\infty}\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-{j_r}}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{j_r}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)=cX_\varnothing$ in $L^2$.
For selected $j$, put $\varepsilon_j=\varepsilon(\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-j}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr),cX_\varnothing)$ and $\varepsilon_j'=\varepsilon(cX_\varnothing,\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-j}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr))$.
Both tend to zero along this subsequence.
Cauchy--Schwarz and uniform fourth inverse moments control the numerators.
The reversed denominator tends to a positive limit by bounded continuity of $\min\{x,x^{-1}\}$ on $(0,\infty)$.


Conditional on $\mathcal F_n$, the boundary pairs $(\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-j}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr),cX)$ are independent across edges.
Their normalised outputs are $\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-{n+j}}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n+j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)$ and $cX_\varnothing$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:electrical-comparison} gives
\[
 \mathbb E[(\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-{n+j}}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n+j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)-cX_\varnothing)_+\mid\mathcal F_n]\le\varepsilon_jc\mathbb E[X_\varnothing\mid\mathcal F_n],
\]
and, in the other direction,
\[\begin{aligned}
 &\mathbb E[(cX_\varnothing-\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-{n+j}}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n+j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr))_+\mid\mathcal F_n]
 \\ &\le\varepsilon_j'\mathbb E[\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-{n+j}}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n+j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\mid\mathcal F_n]
 \\ &\le\varepsilon_j'(\mathbb E \bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-j}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr))\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr).
\end{aligned}\]
The final inequality is conditional concavity.


For either positive-part error, the independent-copy variance identity and Lipschitz continuity of the positive part give conditional variance in expectation at most
\[
 2\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(\bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-{n+j}}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n+j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\mid\mathcal F_n)
 +2c^2\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(X_\varnothing\mid\mathcal F_n)
 \le C\theta^n.
\]
Chebyshev and Borel--Cantelli show that each error differs from its conditional mean by a quantity tending to zero almost surely for fixed selected $j$.
Since $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E[X_\varnothing\mid\mathcal F_n]=X_\varnothing$, $\mathbb E \bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-j}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{j}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\le(\mathbb E X_\varnothing^{-1})$, and $\displaystyle \limsup \bigl(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\le(\mathbb E X_\varnothing^{-1}) X_\varnothing$, the upper limiting errors are at most $\varepsilon_jcX_\varnothing$ and $\varepsilon_j'(\mathbb E X_\varnothing^{-1})^2X_\varnothing$.
Intersect over the countably many selected blocks and let $j\to\infty$ through them.
Each fixed shift covers the whole eventual sequence, proving convergence with $c_{\mathrm R}=c$.


Uniform positive moments give convergence in every finite positive $L^p$. Take the countable address intersection.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:electrical-moment-limits}
For every fixed $t\in\mathbb R$,
$\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-nt}\mathbb E\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)^t=c_{\mathrm R}^{\,t}\mathbb E X_\varnothing^t$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:electrical-amplitudes} gives almost-sure convergence to $c_{\mathrm R}X_\varnothing$. The uniform positive and inverse moment bounds in Lemma~\ref{lem:electrical-uniform-moments} give uniform integrability at every fixed real power, so expectations converge.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:electrical-uniqueness}
The mean-one eigenlaw and eigenvalue are unique among positive eigenlaws with every positive and inverse moment.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:electrical-amplitudes} to the natural eigenlaw.
For any other eigenlaw in the stated class, the sandwich bounds the physical mean between fixed multiples of its eigenvalue to the power $n$.
Its eigenvalue must therefore equal $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}$.
\textcolor{black}{The construction of Lemma~\ref{lem:electrical-field} realises its mean-one endogenous field on the same innovation tree.
The sandwich bounds apply to this field, so the endpoint argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:electrical-compactness} places a deterministic positive multiple of it in the omega-limit set of the same unit-input resistance sequence.
By Theorem~\ref{thm:electrical-amplitudes}, that set is the singleton $\{c_{\mathrm R}X_\varnothing\}$.
Taking expectations identifies the multiple as $c_{\mathrm R}$, and hence the two mean-one fields and their laws agree.}
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:full-resistance-mesh}
Almost surely there are exponentially decreasing bounds $\Gamma_k$ with $\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty}\Gamma_k=0$ for the diameters of every retained generation-$k$ component in $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_n}$, simultaneously for all $n\ge k$.
Each component's normalised diameter supremum has every positive moment.
The assertion includes both sides of $b$ and all one-terminal decorations.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
At connected $u$, put $V_u=\sup_{r\ge0}\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-r}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{u,r}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)$.
It has all positive moments by Lemma~\ref{lem:electrical-uniform-moments}.
Define $H_{u,r}$ as the maximum resistance distance to available terminals in each vertex's own component, using the nearer terminal for $c$ and the maximum of the separate radii for $b$.
The seed radii vanish.
Reach a child terminal and follow a simple active coarse route to a parent terminal.
Resistance triangle inequalities and Rayleigh monotonicity give
\[
 H_{u,r+1}\le\max_{i\text{ retained}}H_{ui,r}
                +\sum_{i:T_{ui}=c}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{ui,r}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-).
\]
Apply this separately to each side of $b$.


As in Lemma~\ref{lem:full-mesh},
\[
 \sup_r\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-r}H_{u,r}
 \le A_u:=m\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-j}
          \max_{\substack{|w|=j\text{ below }u\\T_w=c}}V_w.
\]
For arbitrarily large $p$, its $L^p$ norm is bounded by
$mC_p\sum_{j\ge1}(m^{1/p}/\lambda_{\mathfrak C})^j$.
Thus $G_u=2A_u+\mathbf1_{\{T_u=c\}}V_u$ bounds every normalised component diameter and has all positive moments.
The maximum over at most $m^k$ frontier sockets gives
$\mathbb P(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-k}\max G_u>\eta^k)\le C[m/(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}\eta)^p]^k$
for $m^{1/p}/\lambda_{\mathfrak C}<\eta<1$.
Borel--Cantelli proves the result.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:resistance-metric}
There is a compact resistance metric $R_*$ on the chemical carrier $\mathfrak C$ such that
$(V(\mathfrak C_n),\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-n}\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_n})$ converges almost surely to $(\mathfrak C,R_*)$ in marked Gromov--Hausdorff topology.
The metrics $R_*$ and $d_{\mathrm{ch}}$ induce the same topology.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Work on the event of probability one where the amplitude limits at all addresses and both component mesh bounds hold.
For each connected cell $u$, let $s_u,t_u$ be its planted terminals, and define $\mathcal E_n^0(f):=\sum_{\{x,y\}\in E(\mathfrak C_n)}(f(x)-f(y))^2$, counting each undirected edge once.
Eliminating the interiors of generation-$k$ cells gives
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}_{V_k}(\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n\mathcal E_n^0)(f)
 =\sum_{\substack{|u|=k\\T_u=c}}
 \frac{\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n}{\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{u,n-k}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)}
       (f(s_u)-f(t_u))^2.
\]
A one-root component contributes zero because its boundary value extends constantly over the component.
This applies separately to the two components of a $b$-cell; their interiors reappear on finer skeletons, while connected cells in dangling branches already contribute to the displayed sum.

Theorem~\ref{thm:electrical-amplitudes} gives the limiting finite form
\begin{equation}\label{eq:limiting-trace}
 \mathcal E^{(k)}(f):=
 \sum_{\substack{|u|=k\\T_u=c}}
 \frac{\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^k}{c_{\mathrm R}X_u}
       (f(s_u)-f(t_u))^2.
\end{equation}
The skeleton network is connected and its conductances are positive.
On such a finite network, tracing to a fixed vertex set depends continuously on the conductances, as follows from the finite energy-minimisation problem.
We may therefore pass to the limit in the finite-level trace identity to obtain $\operatorname{Tr}_{V_k}\mathcal E^{(k+1)}=\mathcal E^{(k)}$.
Effective resistance is preserved by tracing, so these forms define a single resistance metric $R_*$ on $V_*$.

To prove compactness, pass the bound in Lemma~\ref{lem:full-resistance-mesh} to each fixed finite set of limiting born vertices.
The generation-$k$ component anchors then form a finite $\Gamma_k$-net in $V_*$, and hence in its resistance completion $\mathfrak C_{\mathrm R}$.
Since $\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty}\Gamma_k=0$, this completion is compact.
Project the finite approximants and the completion to the same labelled anchors.
For fixed $k$, their anchor resistance matrices converge, while each projection moves points by at most $\Gamma_k$.
First taking the limit in $n$ and then in $k$ proves marked resistance Gromov--Hausdorff convergence to $\mathfrak C_{\mathrm R}$.

We next construct the form needed to identify this completion with the chemical carrier.
For a function on $V_*$, define $\mathcal E(f):=\sup_k\mathcal E^{(k)}(f|_{V_k})$; trace compatibility makes these finite energies increasing.
The finite resistance inequalities give $|f(x)-f(y)|^2\le R_*(x,y)\mathcal E(f)$, so every finite-energy function extends continuously to $\mathfrak C_{\mathrm R}$.
Let $\mathcal D$ consist of these extensions.
Harmonic extension from $V_k$ to successive skeletons preserves energy, and uniqueness of each finite minimiser makes the extensions agree on their common vertices.
Clipping a function to $[0,1]$ decreases every finite-network energy; taking the supremum therefore gives the Markov property for $\mathcal E$.
The compatible-sequence theorem \cite[Theorem~2.13]{Kigami2003} supplies the resistance-form axioms on $V_*$ and identifies the associated metric with $R_*$.
Theorem~2.12 of the same reference extends the form to $\mathfrak C_{\mathrm R}$, and Theorem~2.14 shows that its traces on the dense skeletons determine it uniquely.

It remains to identify the two completions.
Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and choose a generation whose resistance mesh is at most $\varepsilon$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:cell-localisation}, its chemical component closures meet only at shared planted vertices.
There are finitely many such compact sets, so the distance between any disjoint pair has a positive lower bound, when disjoint pairs exist.
Consequently, sufficiently chemically close born vertices lie in the same component or in two components sharing a planted vertex, and their resistance distance is at most $2\varepsilon$.
Thus the identity on $V_*$ is uniformly continuous from the chemical metric to $R_*$ and extends to a continuous map $\mathfrak C\to\mathfrak C_{\mathrm R}$.
Its image is compact and contains the dense set $V_*$, so the map is surjective.

For injectivity, take distinct $x,y\in\mathfrak C$ and a generation whose chemical mesh is less than $d_{\mathrm{ch}}(x,y)/4$.
The components containing $x$ and $y$ have disjoint planted boundary sets, since a shared boundary point would put $x$ and $y$ at distance less than $d_{\mathrm{ch}}(x,y)/2$.
Prescribe zero on the first boundary, one on the second, and arbitrary values at the other skeleton vertices, then extend harmonically to the finer skeletons.
The extension has finite energy and is constant on each of the two components: constant boundary data have the constant extension as their energy minimiser.
Its resistance-continuous extension therefore separates the images of $x$ and $y$.
The map is a continuous bijection between compact metric spaces, hence a homeomorphism.
Identifying $\mathfrak C_{\mathrm R}$ with $\mathfrak C$ gives the claimed metric and common topology; the same labelled anchors give the marked convergence on this carrier.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:full-resistance-form}
The finite electrical traces determine a unique regular strongly local resistance form $(\mathcal E,\mathcal D)$ on $\mathfrak C$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The compatible-trace construction in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:resistance-metric} supplies the resistance form and proves uniqueness from its dense traces.

Compact resistance forms are regular \cite[Corollary~6.4]{Kigami2012}.
Here this also follows by harmonic interpolation of a continuous function's values on $V_k$: the maximum principle and vanishing component mesh give uniform approximation.


Suppose $f,g\in\mathcal D$ and $f$ is constant on a neighbourhood $U$ of $\operatorname{supp} g$.
If $\mathfrak C\setminus U$ is nonempty, its chemical distance from $\operatorname{supp} g$ is positive.
For large $k$, every trace edge has endpoints in a component smaller than this distance.
If $g$ differs at the endpoints, one lies in $\operatorname{supp} g$ and both lie in $U$, so the difference of $f$ is zero.
Every mixed trace summand vanishes.
Passing to the limit gives $\mathcal E(f,g)=0$.
If $U=\mathfrak C$ the conclusion is immediate.
Thus the form is strongly local.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:degree-measure}
Both $\frac{1}{|V(\mathfrak C_n)|}\sum_{x\in V(\mathfrak C_n)}\delta_x$ and $\frac{1}{2|E(\mathfrak C_n)|}\sum_{x\in V(\mathfrak C_n)}\deg_{\mathfrak C_n}(x)\delta_x$ converge to the probability measure $\mu$, in the common chemical and resistance realisations.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
With the Perron normalisation of Section~\ref{sec:geometry},
$\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^{-n}|E(\mathfrak C_n)|=v_cW_c$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^{-n}|V(\mathfrak C_n)|=W_c$ almost surely.


Each microscopic $c$ seed contributes one edge; every other seed contributes none.
Thus $|E(\mathfrak C_n)|=Z_{n,c}$ and the edge limit is the Perron limit.
The almost-sure vertex limit is Lemma~\ref{lem:vertex-mass-limit}, with the mass normalisation of IGS~II.
The same edge and birth rewards work inside every fixed component, with the inherited mask for a side of $b$.


Assign each microscopic edge to its unique frontier component and move both endpoint half-masses to its anchor.
The projected degree probability mass is exactly its edge count divided by $|E(\mathfrak C_n)|$, even at old high-degree junctions.
For counting measure use first-birth ownership.
The allocation error involves only finitely many frontier boundary vertices and vanishes after normalisation.
Component edge and vertex ratios tend to the same descendant martingale ratios, because their deterministic reward constants cancel.
These ratios define $\mu$.
Both transports have displacement bounded by the component mesh in either metric.
First let $n\to\infty$ and then let the frontier depth tend to infinity.
Full support was proved in Section~\ref{sec:geometry}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:natural-process}
On one event of probability one, for every starting-vertex sequence converging to $x\in \mathfrak C$, the conditional laws of
$(S^n_{\lfloor2|E(\mathfrak C_n)|\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^nt\rfloor})_{t\ge0}$ converge weakly to $B$ started at $x$, in the Skorokhod $J_1$ topology of a common chemical realisation.
Here $S^n$ is discrete simple random walk.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Fix an environment with all the address-wise limits, both uniform mesh bounds and the mass limits.
Theorem~\ref{thm:full-resistance-form} and Lemma~\ref{lem:degree-measure} give compact measured resistance convergence.
Croydon's theorem \cite[Theorem~1.2]{Croydon2018} applies.
Its escape condition is automatic: the compact convergent spaces have uniformly bounded diameters, so sufficiently large balls contain the entire spaces.
The associated process laws converge weakly in a common resistance embedding.


Use the common component correspondences to realise the chemical spaces in one complete separable space.
They have vanishing resistance distortion and chemical embedding error.
The identity from the limiting resistance space to its chemical carrier is continuous.
These are the spatial conditions of \cite[Theorem~7.1]{Croydon2018}, giving weak $J_1$ convergence of the embedded processes with continuous limiting paths.
The argument is deterministic after fixing the environment.
Every convergent starting sequence supplies a convergent pointed sequence, so the same environment event covers all such sequences.


For the discrete transition matrix $\mathbf P_n$, direct summation gives

\[
 \langle f-\mathbf P_n f,f\rangle_{\frac{1}{2|E(\mathfrak C_n)|}\sum_{x\in V(\mathfrak C_n)}\deg_{\mathfrak C_n}(x)\delta_x}=\mathcal E_n^0(f)/(2|E(\mathfrak C_n)|)\textcolor{black}{.}
\]
Thus the process for $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n\mathcal E_n^0$ and $\frac{1}{2|E(\mathfrak C_n)|}\sum_{x\in V(\mathfrak C_n)}\deg_{\mathfrak C_n}(x)\delta_x$ has generator $2|E(\mathfrak C_n)|\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n(\mathbf P_n-\mathbf I)$.
The factor two comes from counting undirected edges once in the energy.


Attach independent mean-one exponential holding times $\xi_i$.
Set $\sigma_k:=\sum_{i\le k}\xi_i$, $N(t):=\max\{k:\sigma_k\le t\}$ and $Y_n(t):=S^n_{N((2|E(\mathfrak C_n)|\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n)t)}$.
Since $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}2|E(\mathfrak C_n)|\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n=\infty$, both $N((2|E(\mathfrak C_n)|\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n)t)/(2|E(\mathfrak C_n)|\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n)$ and
$\gamma_n(t):=\sigma_{\lfloor (2|E(\mathfrak C_n)|\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n)t\rfloor}/(2|E(\mathfrak C_n)|\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n)$ tend uniformly on compact intervals in probability to $t$.
The identity $Y_n(\gamma_n(t))=S^n_{\lfloor (2|E(\mathfrak C_n)|\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n)t\rfloor}$ holds.
Convergence to a continuous limiting path law and the vanishing clock error give the same weak $J_1$ limit for the discrete walk.
No aperiodicity is required.


\textcolor{black}{Almost-sure metric--measure convergence together with these conditional path-law limits gives quenched Gromov--Hausdorff--Prokhorov--Skorokhod convergence under the clock $2|E(\mathfrak C_n)|\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n$.}
It is not an assertion of almost-sure convergence of the original walk sample paths.
Integration over environments gives the corresponding annealed joint convergence.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:continuous-time-walk}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:natural-process}, rate-one continuous-time simple random walk, accelerated by $2|E(\mathfrak C_n)|\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n$, has the same conditional diffusion limit.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
The Poissonised walk in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:natural-process} is the process associated with the rescaled energy and the degree probability measure. Its convergence is obtained there before removing the exponential holding times.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:variable-speed-walk}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:natural-process}, the continuous-time walk with rate one along each incident edge, accelerated by $|V(\mathfrak C_n)|\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n$, has the same conditional diffusion limit.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
The generator is $L_nf(x)=\sum_{y\sim x}(f(y)-f(x))$. Its energy for the uniform vertex measure is $\mathcal E_n^0/|V(\mathfrak C_n)|$. \textcolor{black}{Acceleration by $|V(\mathfrak C_n)|\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n$ gives $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^n\mathcal E_n^0$,} and the same measured-resistance convergence and spatial comparison used in Theorem~\ref{thm:natural-process} apply.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:deterministic-clock}
Under deterministic acceleration $(\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})\lambda_{\mathfrak C})^n$, simple random walk converges conditionally to $(B_{t/(2v_cW_c)})_{t\ge0}$, equivalently to the resistance-form process with speed measure $2v_cW_c\mu$.
For the variable-speed walk, replace $2v_cW_c$ by $W_c$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
The ratios of deterministic acceleration to the exact clocks tend to $(2v_cW_c)^{-1}$ and $W_c^{-1}$.
These positive limits give convergent linear changes of time.
Multiplying a speed measure by a positive constant divides the generator by that constant.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:spectral-dimension}
Following the diffusion notation of IGS~I, at $x\in \mathfrak C$ the pointwise spectral dimension is
\[
 \dim_{\mathrm S}^{(\mathrm N)}(\mathfrak C:x):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}
 \frac{2\log p_t(x,x)}{\log(1/t)},
\]
when this limit exists.
The resistance dimension relative to the chemical scale is
$\dim_{\mathrm R}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}}):=\log\lambda_{\mathfrak C}/\log\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}$.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:heat-kernels}\label{lem:spectral-typical}
Almost surely, for $\mu$-almost every $x\in \mathfrak C$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:spectral-dimension-form}
 \dim_{\mathrm S}^{(\mathrm N)}(\mathfrak C:x)=\frac{2\log\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})}{\log(\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})\lambda_{\mathfrak C})}
 =\frac{2\dim_{\mathrm B}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})}{\dim_{\mathrm B}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})+\dim_{\mathrm R}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
At the points of Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral-collars}, the containing component has mass $\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^{-k}e^{o(k)}$ and intrinsic resistance diameter at most $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-k}e^{o(k)}$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:resolvent-component} gives
$G_{(\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})\lambda_{\mathfrak C})^k}(x,x)\le\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-k}e^{o(k)}$.


Fix rational $\eta>0$ and $n=\lceil\eta k\rceil$.
Eventually the generation-$(k+n)$ component $D$ containing $x$ does not meet the boundary of $A=A_k(x)$.
On the refined skeleton in $A$, give the roots of $D$ value one and all other vertices value zero.
Extend harmonically within the descendant components and by zero outside $A$.
The finite trace construction gives $f\in\mathcal D$, with $0\le f\le1$ and $f(x)=1$.
For a side of $b$, the other side has its separate boundary prescription on the shared continuation.
There are at most $m^n$ connected refined trace edges inside the parent socket.
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:typical-cutoff}
 \mathcal E(f)\le
 \frac{m^n\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{k+n}}{c_{\mathrm R}}
 \max_{\substack{|u|=k+n\\T_u=c}}X_u^{-1},
 \qquad \|f\|_2^2\le\mu(A).
\end{equation}
Equation~\eqref{eq:spectral-maxima} bounds the energy by
$C_{\omega,\varepsilon}\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^k
 e^{n\log(m\lambda_{\mathfrak C})+\varepsilon(k+n)}$,
whereas $(\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})\lambda_{\mathfrak C})^k\|f\|_2^2\le\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^ke^{o(k)}$.


Insert $f$ in \eqref{eq:resolvent-variational}.
The exponential loss per generation is at most
$\eta\log(m\lambda_{\mathfrak C})+\varepsilon(1+\eta)$.
Take common events for rational parameters and then let $\eta,\varepsilon\downarrow0$.
This proves the lower bound $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-k}e^{-o(k)}$.
Monotonicity interpolates between successive $(\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})\lambda_{\mathfrak C})^k$.
Since $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}^{-k}=((\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})\lambda_{\mathfrak C})^k)^{\log\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})/\log(\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})\lambda_{\mathfrak C})-1}$ and $0<\log\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})/\log(\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})\lambda_{\mathfrak C})<1$, Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral-resolvent} applies.

The resulting diagonal heat-kernel exponent gives the stated spectral dimension by Definition~\ref{def:spectral-dimension}.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:spectral-threshold}
For the fivefold subdivided diamond, the two terminal paths each have length ten.
Its fully open effective resistance is $5$, so Rayleigh monotonicity at every substitution depth gives $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}\ge5$.
The rule has twenty edges, whence $\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})\le20$.
The spectral formula, increasing in $\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})$ and decreasing in $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}>1$, yields
\[
 \dim_{\mathrm S}^{(\mathrm N)}(\mathfrak C)\le\frac{2\log20}{\log20+\log5}
 =\frac{\log20}{\log10}\approx1.3010<\frac43.
\]
This calculation already gives a strict non-AO example without computing the random electrical eigenlaw.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:critical-supersolution}
Suppose $Z\ge0$ is measurable with respect to the innovation tree, $0<\mathbb E Z<\infty$, and $\mathcal T Z\le aZ$ almost surely for a deterministic $a>0$.
Then $a\ge\lambda_{\mathfrak C}$.
If equality holds, $Z$ is a deterministic positive multiple of $X$.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Independent thinning gives
$\mathbb P(Z=0)\le\mathbb P(\mathcal T Z=0)=g(\mathbb P(Z=0))$.
Since $\mathbb E Z>0$ and $g(u)<u$ on $(0,1)$, we have $\mathbb P(Z=0)=0$.
The small-resistance argument in Lemma~\ref{lem:electrical-eigenlaw} also gives
\[
 \mathbb P(Z\le t)\le g\bigl(\mathbb P(Z\le\max\{2,ma\}t)\bigr).
\]
Iteration, starting at any $t_0$ with $\mathbb P(Z\le t_0)<1$, yields every inverse moment of $Z$.

Iterate the supersolution inequality and condition on $\mathcal F_n$.
Concavity of effective conductance, followed by Jensen's inequality for reciprocals, gives
\[
 \mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal F_n]
 \ge a^{-n}\mathbb E[F_{\mathcal H_n}(Z_u)\mid\mathcal F_n]
 \ge\frac{\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)}{a^n\mathbb E Z^{-1}}.
\]
Taking expectations and using Theorem~\ref{thm:resistance-exponent} proves $a\ge\lambda_{\mathfrak C}$.
If $a=\lambda_{\mathfrak C}$, the lower sandwich bound in Lemma~\ref{lem:electrical-sandwich} and martingale convergence imply
$Z\ge X/\mathbb E Z^{-1}$ almost surely.

Let $c:=\operatorname{ess\,sup}(X/Z)$, so $0<c<\infty$.
Superadditivity of resistance shows that the nonnegative integrable function $cZ-X$ satisfies
$\mathcal T(cZ-X)\le\lambda_{\mathfrak C}(cZ-X)$.
If it is nonzero, the preceding argument applied to this function gives
\[
 cZ-X\ge\frac{X}{\mathbb E(cZ-X)^{-1}}.
\]
Consequently $X/Z\le c/(1+1/\mathbb E(cZ-X)^{-1})<c$ almost surely, contradicting the definition of $c$.
Thus $cZ=X$ almost surely.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:strict-chemical-resistance}
For every classical rule,
$1<\lambda_{\mathfrak C}<\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}$.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
The first inequality is Theorem~\ref{thm:resistance-exponent}.
A unit flow along a shortest path with edge costs $X_e^{\mathrm{ch}}$ gives
$\mathcal T X^{\mathrm{ch}}\le\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}X^{\mathrm{ch}}$.
This inequality is strict on the all-open parent event.
Indeed, the terminal mincut is at least two, so a shortest terminal path has an alternative segment joining two of its vertices through edges outside that segment.
Diverting a sufficiently small positive amount of its unit current along the alternative segment decreases the energy: the saving on the original segment is linear in the diverted current, whereas the additional energy is quadratic.
All edge costs are positive, and the all-open event has conditional probability $p_c^{m-1}>0$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:critical-supersolution} therefore rules out $\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}=\lambda_{\mathfrak C}$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:mass-core-clock}
For every classical rule, $\dim_{\mathrm B}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})+\dim_{\mathrm R}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})>2$.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Every core edge is a connected child, so $M_{c,c}\ge\mathbb E|E(H)|$.
Primitivity and the positive right Perron vector of $\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C}$ give $\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})>M_{c,c}$: the $c$ row has a positive off-diagonal entry, corresponding to a live noncrossing child.
Thus $\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})>\mathbb E|E(H)|$.

For any finite network with unit resistances, orient its electrical unit flow along decreasing potential and decompose it into terminal path flows of total weight one.
The sum of the absolute edge currents is at least the shortest terminal distance.
Cauchy--Schwarz therefore gives, for the recursively retained core,
\[
 d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)^2\le |E(\mathcal H_n)|\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-).
\]
Its expected edge count is $(\mathbb E|E(H)|)^n$, by independent reproduction at each core address.
    Taking square roots and expectations gives
\[
 (\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-))^2\le(\mathbb E|E(H)|)^n\mathbb E\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-).
\]
The growth limits in Theorems~\ref{thm:chemical-scalar} and~\ref{thm:resistance-exponent} give $(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^2\le(\mathbb E|E(H)|)\lambda_{\mathfrak C}$.
Combining the two inequalities gives $\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})\lambda_{\mathfrak C}>(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^2$, which is precisely the asserted strict dimension bound.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- aoresult-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:ao-region}
For every classical EIGS rule, if
\[
 (\dim_{\mathrm B}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}}),\dim_{\mathrm R}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}}))
 \notin (\frac{4}{3},2)\times(\frac{2}{3},1),
\]
then the typical spectral dimension of the natural limiting diffusion on its critical cluster satisfies
\[
 \dim_{\mathrm S}^{(\mathrm N)}(\mathfrak C)\neq\frac{4}{3}.
\]
<!-- end aoresult-1 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Lemmas~\ref{lem:strict-chemical-resistance} and~\ref{lem:mass-core-clock} give
$0<\dim_{\mathrm R}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})<1$ and $\dim_{\mathrm B}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})+\dim_{\mathrm R}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})>2$.
If $\dim_{\mathrm S}^{(\mathrm N)}(\mathfrak C)=4/3$, equation~\eqref{eq:ao-equality} gives
$3\dim_{\mathrm R}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})>2$ and $\dim_{\mathrm B}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})=2\dim_{\mathrm R}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})<2$.
Both inequalities are strict, proving the statement including its boundary cases.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:long-diamond-region}
Replace each edge of the standard diamond by a path of five unit edges.
The resulting rule has twenty edges and two terminal paths of length ten, so $\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}=10$.
Since $\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})<20$,
\[
 \dim_{\mathrm B}(\mathfrak C,d_{\mathrm{ch}})<\frac{\log20}{\log10}\approx1.3010<\frac43.
\]
Its typical spectral dimension is therefore strictly smaller than $4/3$ by the preceding sign calculation.
The critical point throughout is that of this subdivided rule.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:spectral-density}
The typical spectral dimensions $\dim_{\mathrm S}^{(\mathrm N)}(\mathfrak C)$ of the natural limiting diffusions on critical percolation clusters of classical EIGS hierarchical lattices are dense in $(1,2)$.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
See Appendix~\ref{app:spectral-density}.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- aoconjecture-1: body_md -->
\label{conj:ao-global}
For every classical EIGS hierarchical lattice at its own critical point, the typical spectral dimension of the natural limiting diffusion on the full terminal-connected cluster satisfies
\[
\dim_{\mathrm S}^{(\mathrm N)}(\mathfrak C) \neq \frac{4}{3}.
\]
That is, the Alexander-Orbach conjecture does not hold on any classical EIGS hierarchical lattice.
<!-- end aoconjecture-1 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:chemical-moments}
The laws of $d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)/(\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-))$ have uniformly bounded moments of every fixed positive and negative order.
There is a mean-one law on $(0,\infty)$ and $\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}>1$ such that $F_H^{\mathrm{ch}}(X_e^{\mathrm{ch}})$ has the law of $\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}} X^{\mathrm{ch}}$ for independent child copies.
This law has every positive and negative moment.
For each finite $t>0$, $\mathbb E e^{tX^{\mathrm{ch}}}$ and $\sup_n\mathbb E e^{td_{\mathfrak C_n}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)/(\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-))}$ are finite.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Under $\mathcal Q_c$, the pivotal bonds counted by $N_{\mathrm{piv}}(R)$ in IGS~II are precisely the open edges present in every terminal path.
The conditional pivotal-count identity in \textcolor{black}{\cite[proof of Lemma~2.16]{NeroliIGSII2026}} gives $\mathbb E N_{\mathrm{piv}}(R)=\varphi_R'(p_c)>1$.
For independent mean-one nonnegative inputs, their sum is a lower bound for $F_H^{\mathrm{ch}}$.
Choose a deterministic simple path in each $H$, independently of the inputs, and let its length be $J(H)$.
Then $\mathbb E J(H)\le L$.
For any mean-one input law $\nu$ we obtain $\varphi_R'(p_c)\le \mathbb E F_H^{\mathrm{ch}}(X_e^{\mathrm{ch}})\le\mathbb E J(H)$.
This lower bound is $\varphi_R'(p_c)$, rather than a pathwise assertion that arbitrary weighted paths cost at least $\ell$.

These first-moment bounds allow us to construct an invariant class of laws.
Let $\widehat T\nu$ be the law of $F_H^{\mathrm{ch}}(X_e^{\mathrm{ch}})/(\mathbb E F_H^{\mathrm{ch}}(X_e^{\mathrm{ch}}))$.
For integer $p\ge2$, interpolation gives $\mathbb E (X^{\mathrm{ch}})^r\le \bigl(\mathbb E (X^{\mathrm{ch}})^p\bigr)^{(r-1)/(p-1)}$ for $1\le r\le p$.
The pure terms in a selected-path multinomial expansion contribute $(\mathbb E J(H))\bigl(\mathbb E (X^{\mathrm{ch}})^p\bigr)$.
A mixed monomial with $k\ge2$ distinct variables is bounded by $\bigl(\mathbb E (X^{\mathrm{ch}})^p\bigr)^{(p-k)/(p-1)}$.
Consequently
\[
 \int_0^\infty x^p\,(\widehat T\nu)(dx)\le \frac{\mathbb E J(H)}{\varphi_R'(p_c)^p}\left(\int_0^\infty x^p\,\nu(dx)\right)
       +A_p\left(\int_0^\infty x^p\,\nu(dx)\right)^{(p-2)/(p-1)}
\]
for a finite $A_p$.
For all sufficiently large integers $p$, choose $K_p\ge1$ so that this bound preserves $\bigl(\mathbb E (X^{\mathrm{ch}})^p\bigr)\le K_p$.
The mean-one laws satisfying these constraints form a nonempty convex weakly compact set.
Higher moments ensure tightness and preservation of the mean; lower semicontinuity preserves the constraints.
The Lipschitz bound for $F_H^{\mathrm{ch}}$ and uniform integrability make $\widehat T$ continuous there.
Schauder's theorem gives a fixed law with eigenvalue $\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}=\mathbb E F_H^{\mathrm{ch}}(X_e^{\mathrm{ch}})\in[\varphi_R'(p_c),\mathbb E J(H)]$.
It has every positive moment.
Iteration from $\delta_1$ gives the corresponding uniform moments of $d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)/(\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-))$.

To control negative moments, we estimate the probability of small values.
If $z=\mathbb P(X^{\mathrm{ch}}=0)$, then $z=g(z)$, since zero terminal cost is a crossing through zero-cost child edges.
This is independent thinning of a crossing Bernoulli-$p_c$ configuration.
The mean excludes $z=1$, and $g(u)<u$ for $0<u<1$ excludes $0<z<1$.
Thus $X^{\mathrm{ch}}>0$.
For $F(t):=\mathbb P(X^{\mathrm{ch}}\le t)$, a path with cost at most $\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}} t$ uses only edges of cost at most $\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}} t$.
Hence $F(t)\le g(F(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}} t))$.
Choosing $F(t_0)<1$ and iterating gives $F(t_0(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-k})\le\exp(-c\ell^k)$ after finitely many initial terms.
This proves every inverse moment.

For
\[
 F_n(t):=\mathbb P(d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)/(\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-))\le t)
\]
, the bound
\[
 (\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n+1}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-))/(\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-))\le L
\]
 gives $F_{n+1}(t)\le g(F_n(Lt))$.
Uniform second moments and Paley--Zygmund give $F_n(1/2)\le r<1$.
For $n\ge k$, $F_n((1/2)L^{-k})\le g^{\circ k}(r)$.
For $n<k$, the event is empty because
\[
 d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)/(\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-))\ge(\ell/L)^n>(1/2)L^{-k}\textcolor{black}{.}
\]
The same small-ball estimate is therefore uniform over $n$.

We next strengthen the positive-moment estimates to factorial bounds.
Choose $p_0$ so that $\binom{p+L-1}{L-1}<\varphi_R'(p_c)^p$ for $p\ge p_0$.
Choose $A\ge1$ to cover the finitely many lower-order moment bounds by $A^r r!$.
If the bound holds below order $p$, each mixed multinomial term is at most $A^pp!$.
A path of length $J$ has at most $\binom{p+L-1}{L-1}-J$ mixed terms.
Thus
\[\begin{aligned}
 &\mathbb E\left(\frac{d_{\mathfrak C_{n+1}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)}{\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n+1}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)}\right)^p\\
 &\quad\le \varphi_R'(p_c)^{-p}(\mathbb E J(H))\mathbb E\left(\frac{d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)}{\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)}\right)^p\\
 &\qquad{}+\varphi_R'(p_c)^{-p}A^pp!\left(\binom{p+L-1}{L-1}-\mathbb E J(H)\right).
\end{aligned}\]
Induction on $p$ and then $n$ yields $\mathbb E\left(\frac{d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)}{\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)}\right)^p\le A^pp!$.
For the eigenlaw, $((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^p-\mathbb E J(H))\bigl(\mathbb E (X^{\mathrm{ch}})^p\bigr)\le A^pp!(\binom{p+L-1}{L-1}-\mathbb E J(H))$ gives the same bound because $(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^p\ge \varphi_R'(p_c)^p>\binom{p+L-1}{L-1}$.

The factorial bounds first give exponential moments on a right neighbourhood of zero.
If $\psi_n(t):=\mathbb E e^{td_{\mathfrak C_n}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)/(\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-))}$, the path bound and $(\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n+1}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-))/(\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-))\ge \varphi_R'(p_c)$ give $\psi_{n+1}(\varphi_R'(p_c)t)\le\psi_n(t)^L$.
Together with $\psi_0(t)=e^t$, this extends uniform finiteness from $t$ to $\varphi_R'(p_c)t$.
Iteration reaches every finite positive $t$.
The eigenlaw obeys the analogous bound $\psi(\varphi_R'(p_c)t)\le\psi(t)^L$.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:chemical-paths}
There is $C_R<\infty$ such that a realised depth-$n$ path-core graph has at most $C_R^k$ simple terminal paths of $k$ microscopic edges.
If $\theta>0$ and independent leaf costs $U\ge0$ satisfy $C_Re^{\theta v}\mathbb E e^{-\theta U}<1$, then
\[
 \mathbb P\{F_{\mathcal H_n}^{\mathrm{ch}}(U)<vd_{\mathfrak C_n}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\mid\mathcal H_n\}\le\frac{(C_Re^{\theta v}\mathbb E e^{-\theta U})^{\ell^n}}{1-C_Re^{\theta v}\mathbb E e^{-\theta U}}.
\]
For $\theta>0$ and pairs $(U,V)$ independent across leaves, $C_R\mathbb E e^{\theta(U-cV)}<1$ gives the same bound with $C_R\mathbb E e^{\theta(U-cV)}$ in place of $C_Re^{\theta v}\mathbb E e^{-\theta U}$ for the event that some terminal path has $\sum U>c\sum V$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
A simple microscopic terminal path cannot revisit a planted vertex or re-enter a two-terminal child after leaving it.
It therefore projects recursively to simple coarse terminal paths.
Its ordered encoding tree has $k$ leaves and between $\ell$ and $L$ children at each internal vertex.
There are at most $k-1$ internal vertices.
The number of such plane trees is exponential in $k$, and each internal label has only finitely many possible oriented rule paths.
This gives $C_R^k$ after increasing the constant.
