For a fixed path of $k$ leaves, exponential Markov bounds $\mathbb P(\sum U<vk)$ by $(e^{\theta v}\mathbb E e^{-\theta U})^k$.
Sum over all paths and $k\ge\ell^n$.
If every path costs at least $v$ times its length, the minimum is at least $vd_{\mathfrak C_n}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)$.
Applying the same calculation to $U-cV$ gives the paired assertion.
The coordinates of each pair can be dependent.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:chemical-compactness}
The eigenlaw has a stationary realisation measurable with respect to the original innovation tree.
There are deterministic finite $C,C'$ such that
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 1\le\mathbb E \bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\le C,\qquad
 \sup_n\mathbb E e^{t\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)}<\infty\ (t>0),\qquad
 \\
 X^{\mathrm{ch}}\le\liminf_n\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\le\limsup_n\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\le C'X^{\mathrm{ch}}
 \quad\text{almost surely}.
 \end{gathered}
\]
The sequence is relatively compact in this same $L^2$ probability space.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Sample independent eigenlaw variables at a finite boundary and recurse upwards.
The eigenlaw identity makes the finite-dimensional distributions consistent.
Kolmogorov extension gives a stationary recursive field satisfying $F_{H_u}^{\mathrm{ch}}(X_{ui}^{\mathrm{ch}})=\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}} X_u^{\mathrm{ch}}$, with independent descendant subtrees.
We now remove its possible extra boundary randomness.


Let $\mathcal F_k$ be the first $k$ innovation generations.
For a fixed outer graph and independent positive costs $Y_i$, put $Z=F_{\mathcal H_k}^{\mathrm{ch}}(Y)$ and choose a geodesic $P(Y)$ by deterministic tie-breaking.
Replacing $Y_i$ by an independent $Y_i'$ increases $Z$ by at most $\mathbf1_{\{i\in P(Y)\}}Y_i'$.
The one-sided Efron--Stein inequality gives
\[
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid\mathcal F_k)\le \mathbb E Y^2\,\mathbb E|P(Y)|.
\]
Since $|P(Y)|\le Z\max_iY_i^{-1}$ and there are at most $m^k$ leaves, Cauchy--Schwarz and a maximum bound give
\[
 \mathbb E|P(Y)|\le\|Z\|_2m^{k/p}\|Y^{-1}\|_p\qquad(p\ge2).
\]
With $Y=X^{\mathrm{ch}}$ the output is $(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^kX^{\mathrm{ch}}$.
Choose $p$ with $m^{1/p}<\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:chemical-endogeny}
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(X^{\mathrm{ch}}\mid\mathcal F_k)\le C_0(m^{1/p}/\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^k.
\end{equation}
Thus $X^{\mathrm{ch}}$ is measurable with respect to all innovations.
The same holds at each address; this property is called endogeny \cite{AldousBandyopadhyay2005}.


Conditional concavity gives $\mathbb E[X^{\mathrm{ch}}\mid\mathcal F_n]\le \bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)$.
Martingale convergence implies $X^{\mathrm{ch}}\le\displaystyle \liminf \bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)$, and $\mathbb E \bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\ge1$.
Choose $\theta,v>0$ with $r=C_Re^{\theta v}\mathbb E e^{-\theta X^{\mathrm{ch}}}<1$, using $X^{\mathrm{ch}}>0$.
The stationary identity and Lemma~\ref{lem:chemical-paths} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:chemical-exception}
 \mathbb P(\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)>X^{\mathrm{ch}}/v)\le C_1r^{\ell^n}.
\end{equation}
On this event use $\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\le(L/\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^n$.
It follows that $\mathbb E \bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\le v^{-1}+C_1(L/\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^nr^{\ell^n}$, uniformly bounded.
Borel--Cantelli gives $\displaystyle \limsup \bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\le X^{\mathrm{ch}}/v$.
Since $(\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-))\ge\ell^n$, bounded means also force $\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}\ge\ell$.
The uniform bound on $(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}\mathbb E d_{\mathfrak C_n}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)$ therefore transfers the exponential bounds of Lemma~\ref{lem:chemical-moments} to the chemically rescaled terminal distances.


For $n\ge k$, condition on $\mathcal F_k$ and use independent inputs $Y=\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-{n-k}}d_{\mathfrak C_{n-k}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)$.
Their positive and inverse moments are uniform, by the preceding mean bounds.
The output is $(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^k\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)$, and the same variance estimate gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:chemical-compactness}
 \sup_{n\ge k}\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}(\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\mid\mathcal F_k)\le C_2(m^{1/p}/\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^k.
\end{equation}
For $n<k$ the conditional variance is zero.
Each $\mathcal F_k$ has finitely many atoms, so its bounded conditional expectations lie in a relatively compact finite-dimensional set.
Equation~\eqref{eq:chemical-compactness} approximates the whole sequence uniformly by these sets.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:chemical-endpoint}
The $L^2$ omega-limit set $\mathcal O$ of $(\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr))$ contains $cX^{\mathrm{ch}}$ for a deterministic $c\ge1$.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
The Lipschitz bound makes $T$ continuous in $L^2$.
Compactness gives a nonempty compact $\mathcal O$ with $T\mathcal O=\mathcal O$; the reverse inclusion follows by taking convergent predecessor subsequences.
Each $h\in\mathcal O$ satisfies $X^{\mathrm{ch}}\le h\le C'X^{\mathrm{ch}}$ almost surely, by a further almost-surely convergent subsequence.
Let $c:=\sup_{h\in\mathcal O}\operatorname{ess\,sup}(h/X^{\mathrm{ch}})$.


Suppose $cX^{\mathrm{ch}}\notin\mathcal O$ and consider the nonnegative differences $cX^{\mathrm{ch}}-h$.
Compactness gives $\delta>0$ such that $\inf_h\mathbb E (cX^{\mathrm{ch}}-h)\ge\delta$, since otherwise a convergent subsequence would have limit $cX^{\mathrm{ch}}$.
The second moments have a common finite bound $M$.
Paley--Zygmund gives $\sup_h\mathbb P((cX^{\mathrm{ch}}-h)\le\delta/2)\le1-\delta^2/(4M)<1$.
Superadditivity yields $(cX^{\mathrm{ch}}-Th)\ge T(cX^{\mathrm{ch}}-h)$.
With $Q(t):=\sup_h\mathbb P((cX^{\mathrm{ch}}-h)\le t)$, predecessor invariance and thinning give $Q(t)\le g(Q(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}} t))$.
Thus $\displaystyle\lim_{t\downarrow0}Q(t)=0$.
The inequality $\sup_h\mathbb E e^{-\theta (cX^{\mathrm{ch}}-h)}\le Q(t)+e^{-\theta t}$ proves uniform decay of these Laplace transforms as $\theta\to\infty$.
Choose $\theta,v>0$ with $C_Re^{\theta v}\sup_h\mathbb E e^{-\theta (cX^{\mathrm{ch}}-h)}<1$.


For fixed $h$, choose deterministic predecessor functions $h_{-n}\in\mathcal O$ with $T^nh_{-n}=h$.
Then $(cX^{\mathrm{ch}}-h)\ge T^n(cX^{\mathrm{ch}}-h_{-n})$.
Their leaf copies are independent and independent of the exposed outer graph.
The uniform path bound and Borel--Cantelli give $(cX^{\mathrm{ch}}-h)\ge v\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)$ eventually, hence $(cX^{\mathrm{ch}}-h)\ge vX^{\mathrm{ch}}$.
The constant $v$ is common to all $h$.
Apply the conclusion on a countable dense subset and use closedness of the order inequality.
Every $h\in\mathcal O$ then obeys $h\le(c-v)X^{\mathrm{ch}}$, contradicting the definition of $c$.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:full-mesh}
For every live type, the supremum over all remaining depths of each $\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}$-normalised retained-component diameter has every finite positive moment.
Almost surely there are exponentially decreasing bounds $\Gamma_k$ with $\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty}\Gamma_k=0$ for all generation-$k$ intrinsic component diameters in $(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_n}$, simultaneously for all $n\ge k$.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Equation~\eqref{eq:chemical-exception} and $\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\le(L/\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^n$ give
\[
 V:=\sup_n\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)\le X^{\mathrm{ch}}/v+\sum_{n\ge0}(L/\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^n\mathbf1_{\{\bigl((\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-n}d_{\mathfrak C_{n}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)\bigr)>X^{\mathrm{ch}}/v\}}.
\]
Minkowski and the bound $C_1r^{\ell^n}$ show that $V$ has all positive moments.


Let $H_{u,r}$ be the maximum distance to an available terminal in a vertex's own retained component.
For $c$, minimise over the two terminals; for $b$, take the larger of the separate one-root radii.
The seed radii are zero.
Reach an available child terminal and follow a simple active coarse route to an available parent terminal.
Only connected children provide through-routes.
This yields
\[
 H_{u,r+1}\le\max_iH_{ui,r}+\sum_{i:T_{ui}=c}d_{\mathfrak C_{ui,r}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-).
\]
A possible crossing of the initial connected child is included in the sum.
Iteration gives
\[
 \sup_r(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-r}H_{u,r}
 \le A_u:=m\sum_{j\ge1}(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-j}
          \max_{\substack{|w|=j\text{ below }u\\T_w=c}}V_w.
\]
An empty maximum is zero.
Conditional marginal moment bounds and Minkowski give
$\|A_u\|_p\le m\|V\|_p\sum_{j\ge1}(m^{1/p}/\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^j<\infty$ for arbitrarily large $p$.
Thus all positive orders are finite.
The variable $G_u=2A_u+\mathbf1_{\{T_u=c\}}V_u$ bounds the diameter supremum for each component.
No independence of sibling types is used.


Put $\Gamma_k:=(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}})^{-k}\max_{|u|=k,\;u\text{ live}}G_u$.
For $m^{1/p}/\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}<\eta<1$, Markov gives
$\mathbb P(\Gamma_k>\eta^k)\le C[m/(\ell_{\mathfrak C}^{\mathrm{ch}}\eta)^p]^k$.
Choose $p$ large and apply Borel--Cantelli.
The supremum over remaining depths was already taken in $G_u$, proving the required uniformity.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:spectral-moments}
For each $\varepsilon>0$, almost surely,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:spectral-maxima}
 \max_{A\in\mathcal A_k}(Y_A+H_A)
 +\max_{\substack{|u|=k\\T_u=c}}X_u^{-1}
 \le C_{\omega,\varepsilon}e^{\varepsilon k}\qquad(k\ge0).
\end{equation}
An empty maximum is zero.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
There are at most $m^k$ sockets and two components per socket.
For each variable in \eqref{eq:spectral-maxima}, a moment bound gives frontier exceedance probability at most $C_pm^ke^{-p\varepsilon k}$.
Choose $p\varepsilon>\log m$ and apply Borel--Cantelli.
An intersection over positive rational $\varepsilon$ proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:collar-expected-mass}
There is $C<\infty$ with $\mathbb E[W_c\mu(C_{k,n})]\le C(d_R/\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C}))^n$ for all $k,n$.
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Each substitution multiplies the geometric socket degree at a planted vertex by $d_R$.
At most $2d_R^n$ descendant sockets contribute to the collar of one component.
For a side of $b$ its mass is bounded by the whole socket mass.
Conditional expected continuation masses are at most $\max_\sigma h_\sigma$, while $\mathbb E|\mathbf Z_k|\le C_0\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^k$.
Subadditivity gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:collar-mass}
 \mathbb E[W_c\mu(C_{k,n})]\le C_1\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^kd_R^n\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^{-k-n}
 =C_1(d_R/\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C}))^n.
\end{equation}
This does not require independent $b$ sides or prior mass additivity at boundaries.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{lem:skeleton-zero-mass}
Almost surely, $\mu(V_*)=0$.
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Every retained vertex born by generation $k$ lies in $C_{k,n}$ for every $n$.
Since $\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})>d_R$, \eqref{eq:collar-mass} gives $\mathbb E[W_c\mu(V_k)]=0$.
Countably many generations and $W_c>0$ give $\mu(V_*)=0$.
Components meet only at planted vertices, so their masses are additive and the containing component is unique outside $V_*$.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{lem:spectral-collars}
On one event of probability one, for $\mu$-almost every $x$, its unique generation-$k$ component $A_k(x)$ has $\mu(A_k(x))=\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^{-k}e^{o(k)}$.
For each positive rational $\eta$, such points lie outside $C_{k,\lceil\eta k\rceil}$ eventually.
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
The union $B_k(\varepsilon)$ of components with $Y_A<e^{-\varepsilon k}$ has
\[
 \mathbb E[W_c\mu(B_k(\varepsilon))]
 \le\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})^{-k}e^{-\varepsilon k}\mathbb E[2|\mathbf Z_k|]
 \le C_2e^{-\varepsilon k}.
\]
Tonelli and division by $W_c>0$ give summability of $\mu(B_k(\varepsilon))$ almost surely.
Measure Borel--Cantelli implies eventual avoidance at almost every point.
Together with \eqref{eq:spectral-maxima} and countably many rational $\varepsilon$, this proves the mass asymptotic.
No negative moment of the branching mass is used.


For fixed rational $\eta>0$, \eqref{eq:collar-mass} with $n=\lceil\eta k\rceil$ is summable over $k$.
The same argument proves eventual collar avoidance.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{lem:heat-kernel-continuity}
The heat kernel is jointly continuous.
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Averaging the resistance inequality gives
$|f(x)|^2\le2\|f\|_2^2+2\operatorname{diam}_{R_*}(\mathfrak C)\mathcal E(f)$.
A bounded set for the form norm is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous by
$|f(x)-f(y)|^2\le R_*(x,y)\mathcal E(f)$.
Arzelà--Ascoli gives compact form embedding into $L^2(\mu)$.
Let $(\zeta_j,\phi_j)$ be its spectral decomposition.
The eigenfunctions are continuous, $\displaystyle\lim_{j\to\infty}\zeta_j=\infty$, and bounded point evaluation gives
$\sum_j\phi_j(x)^2/(1+\zeta_j)\le C$ uniformly in $x$.
\textcolor{black}{For $t\ge t_0>0$, the diagonal tail after index $n$ is bounded uniformly in $x$ by $C\sup_{j>n}(1+\zeta_j)e^{-t_0\zeta_j}$.
This bound tends to zero as $n$ tends to infinity.}
Cauchy--Schwarz bounds off-diagonal tails.
Thus $\sum_je^{-t\zeta_j}\phi_j(x)\phi_j(y)$ defines a jointly continuous semigroup kernel.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{lem:resolvent-variational}
For $s>0$ and $x\in \mathfrak C$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:resolvent-variational}
 G_s(x,x)=\sup_{f\in\mathcal D,\;f\ne0}
 \frac{f(x)^2}{\mathcal E(f)+s\|f\|_{L^2(\mu)}^2}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
\textcolor{black}{For every $s>0$, $\mathcal E+s\|\cdot\|_2^2$ is the square of a norm equivalent to the form norm, and point evaluation is bounded for this norm.
Full support of $\mu$ makes the denominator in \eqref{eq:resolvent-variational} positive for every nonzero $f\in\mathcal D$.
The supremum is therefore the squared dual norm of point evaluation.
Spectral expansion identifies it with $\sum_j\phi_j(x)^2/(s+\zeta_j)$; Tonelli's theorem identifies this sum with the Laplace transform of the nonnegative diagonal heat series.}
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{lem:resolvent-component-bound}
For a positive-mass component $A$ containing $x$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:resolvent-component}
 G_s(x,x)\le2\max\left\{\frac1{s\mu(A)},
               \operatorname{diam}^{\mathrm{intr}}_{R_*}(A)\right\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
For $y\in A$, the local resistance inequality gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:component-evaluation}
 |f(x)|^2\le\frac2{\mu(A)}\int_Af^2\,d\mu
       +2\operatorname{diam}^{\mathrm{intr}}_{R_*}(A)\mathcal E_A^{\mathrm g}(f)
\end{equation}
after averaging.
Since the local energy is at most the global energy, this proves \eqref{eq:resolvent-component}.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{lem:spectral-resolvent}
For $0<\beta<1$, a resolvent asymptotic $G_s(x,x)=s^{\beta-1+o(1)}$ implies $p_t(x,x)=t^{-\beta+o(1)}$.
Two-sided constant-factor resolvent bounds imply the corresponding constant-factor heat-kernel bounds.
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
The diagonal spectral series is nonincreasing in time.
Thus $p_t(x,x)\le eG_{1/t}(x,x)/t$.
The assumed resolvent estimate gives
$p_u(x,x)\le C_\varepsilon u^{-\beta-\varepsilon}$ for small $u$.
Splitting the Laplace integral at $t$ gives
$G_s(x,x)\le C_\varepsilon't^{1-\beta-\varepsilon}+s^{-1}p_t(x,x)$.
Choose $0<\varepsilon<\min\{\beta,(1-\beta)/2\}$, put
$s=t^{-(1-\beta-2\varepsilon)/(1-\beta+\varepsilon)}$.
The lower resolvent bound gives
$G_s(x,x)\ge t^{1-\beta-2\varepsilon}$ for small $t$.
The first upper-bound term is negligible.
Hence $p_t(x,x)\ge\frac12t^{-(1-\beta-2\varepsilon)(\beta-\varepsilon)/(1-\beta+\varepsilon)}$ eventually.
Let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$.


The same inequality gives the heat upper bound $Ct^{-\beta}$.
For a resolvent lower bound $G_{1/t}(x,x)\ge ct^{1-\beta}$, split the integral at $\delta t$.
Its first part is at most $C'\delta^{1-\beta}t^{1-\beta}$.
Choose fixed small $\delta$ to make this at most half the lower bound.
The remaining part is at most $t\,p_{\delta t}(x,x)$.
This gives the matching lower bound after a fixed time change.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Fix a rational number $B>1$.
For each sufficiently large integer $t$, take a series chain of $\lceil B^t\rceil$ blocks, each consisting of $\lceil t(4/3)^t\rceil$ internally disjoint paths of length $t$.
Add one edge at each end of this chain, and place a separate path of length two in parallel with the extended chain.
Use the resulting graph as the same deterministic rule at every substitution step.
It is finite, simple and canonical, and reflection exchanges its terminals.
The short and long branches give two edge-disjoint terminal paths, whereas each terminal has degree two.
Thus its terminal distance, terminal degrees and terminal mincut are all two.

All probabilities below use this rule's own critical parameter $p_c$.
Its critical equation is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:density-critical}
 \left[1-(1-p_c^t)^{\lceil t(4/3)^t\rceil}\right]^{\lceil B^t\rceil}
 =\frac{1}{p_c(1+p_c)}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the full reliability is the short-path probability $p^2$ plus $(1-p^2)p^2$ times the chain-crossing probability.
The left side of \eqref{eq:density-critical} is strictly increasing in $p_c$, and the right side is strictly decreasing.
For all sufficiently large $t$, $7/10<p_c<4/5$.
At $p=7/10$, one block crosses with probability at most $2t(14/15)^t<1/2$, whereas the right side of \eqref{eq:density-critical} is $100/119$.
At $p=4/5$, the mean number of successful paths in a block is at least $t(16/15)^t$.
Once $(16/15)^t\ge B$, a union bound makes the entire chain's failure probability at most
$2B^te^{-tB}\le2e^{-t}<11/36$.
This gives the upper endpoint, where the right side is $25/36$.

Let $J$ be the number of successful paths in one block before conditioning.
It has distribution $\operatorname{Bin}(\lceil t(4/3)^t\rceil,p_c^t)$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:density-critical} implies
\[
 \mathbb P(J>0)>\frac{25}{36},
 \qquad
 \frac{1}{8\lceil B^t\rceil}<\mathbb P(J=0)<\frac{1}{\lceil B^t\rceil}.
\]
For the first failure bound, the chain fails with probability greater than $19/119>1/8$, and a union bound applies over its blocks.
For the second, a block failure probability at least $1/\lceil B^t\rceil$ would make the chain-crossing probability at most $e^{-1}<25/36$.
Using $(1-p_c^t)^{\lceil t(4/3)^t\rceil}\le e^{-\mathbb E J}$ and, eventually, $p_c^t<1/2$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:density-path-count}
 \frac{t\log B}{2}<\mathbb E J
 <\log(8\lceil B^t\rceil)<(\lceil B\rceil+2)t,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E[J\mid J>0]<2(\lceil B\rceil+2)t.
\end{equation}
The lower bound follows from
$-\log(1-p_c^t)\le2p_c^t$ and the upper bound on $\mathbb P(J=0)$.

We next bound the natural resistance factor from below, uniformly in recursive depth.
\textcolor{black}{Give the successful edges independent positive resistances with a common finitely supported law $Y$, independent of their statuses, where $\mathbb E Y=1$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)\le8$.
Such laws include the normalised resistances at every finite recursive depth.}
For independent copies along a path,
\[
 \mathbb E e^{-Y/18}\le1-\frac1{18}+\frac9{2\cdot18^2}=\frac{23}{24},
 \qquad
 \mathbb P\left(\sum_{i=1}^tY_i<\frac t2\right)
 \le\left(\frac{69}{70}\right)^t.
\]
Here exponential Markov and $e^{1/36}\le36/35$ give the second estimate.
Let $U$ be the resistance of a block conditioned on crossing.
Given $J=j>0$, with probability at least $1-j(69/70)^t$ every successful path has resistance at least $t/2$.
Parallel addition and Jensen's inequality therefore give
\[
 \mathbb E U\ge\frac t2\mathbb E[J^{-1}\mid J>0]
          -\frac t2\left(\frac{69}{70}\right)^t
 >\frac{1}{4(\lceil B\rceil+2)}
          -\frac t2\left(\frac{69}{70}\right)^t
 >\frac{1}{8(\lceil B\rceil+2)}
\]
for sufficiently large $t$.
Choosing the first successful path bounds $\mathbb E U^2$ by $t^2+8t$.

Let $V$ be the resistance of the extended long branch conditioned on crossing, and let $Z$ be the resistance of the whole rule conditioned on crossing.
Under the long-branch conditioning, the blocks and exterior-edge inputs are independent, so
\[
 \mathbb E V>\frac{\lceil B^t\rceil}{8(\lceil B\rceil+2)},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(V)\le16+\lceil B^t\rceil(t^2+8t).
\]
\textcolor{black}{Before conditioning on whole-rule crossing, the short-branch status is independent of the long-branch states and resistances.
The whole rule crosses with probability $p_c$, whereas the short branch crosses with probability $p_c^2$.
Thus, given whole-rule crossing, the short branch crosses with probability $p_c^2/p_c=p_c$.
On this event, its two input resistances remain independent with law $Y$; their sum bounds $Z$ from above and has second moment $2\mathbb E Y^2+2(\mathbb E Y)^2\le20$.
On the complementary event, of conditional probability $1-p_c$, the short branch fails and the long branch crosses.
By the independence before conditioning, the long-branch resistance on this event has the law of $V$, and it equals the whole-rule resistance.}
Consequently
\[
 \mathbb E Z\ge(1-p_c)\mathbb E V,\qquad
 \mathbb E Z^2\le20p_c+(1-p_c)\bigl((\mathbb E V)^2+\operatorname{Var}(V)\bigr).
\]
Dividing by the squared mean lower bound yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:density-variance}
 \frac{\operatorname{Var}(Z)}{(\mathbb E Z)^2}
 <4+\frac{1600(\lceil B\rceil+2)^2(t^2+8t+36)}{\lceil B^t\rceil}
 <8
\end{equation}
for sufficiently large $t$.
\textcolor{black}{All choices of sufficiently large $t$ above depend only on $B$, uniformly over the finitely supported input laws with the stated two moments.
Fix one such $t$.
Starting from unit input, apply the estimate at depth $n$ with $Y$ distributed as $\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_n}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)/\mathbb E\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_n}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)$.
The exact cell recursion and homogeneity identify the output $Z$ with $\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n+1}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)/\mathbb E\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_n}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)$ in law.
Thus \eqref{eq:density-variance} preserves the variance bound at depth $n+1$, while $\mathbb E Z>\lceil B^t\rceil/[40(\lceil B\rceil+2)]$ gives}
{\color{black}
\[
 \frac{\mathbb E\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_{n+1}}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)}{\mathbb E\mathscr{R}_{\mathfrak C_n}(\mathfrak v_+,\mathfrak v_-)}
 \ge\frac{\lceil B^t\rceil}{40(\lceil B\rceil+2)}.
\]
}
\textcolor{black}{Induction and Theorem~\ref{thm:resistance-exponent}, applied to this fixed rule, yield $\lambda_{\mathfrak C}\ge\lceil B^t\rceil/[40(\lceil B\rceil+2)]$.}

For an upper bound, use unit inputs in one generation.
The binomial identity
\[
 \mathbb E\frac1{J+1}
 =\frac{1-(1-p_c^t)^{\lceil t(4/3)^t\rceil+1}}
        {(\lceil t(4/3)^t\rceil+1)p_c^t}
 \le\frac1{\mathbb E J}
\]
and $j^{-1}\le2/(j+1)$ for $j\ge1$ imply
$\mathbb E[J^{-1}\mid J>0]\le4/\mathbb E J$.
The successful block then has resistance $t/J$, so \eqref{eq:density-path-count} gives $\mathbb E U<8/\log B$.
Routing along the short branch when it crosses and otherwise along the long branch bounds the whole one-generation mean by $2+8\lceil B^t\rceil/\log B$.
Concavity and homogeneity of resistance bound every subsequent mean-growth factor by this unit-input mean.
Theorem~\ref{thm:resistance-exponent} and the lower bound above now give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:density-resistance-asymptotic}
 \frac{\lceil B^t\rceil}{40(\lceil B\rceil+2)}
 \le\lambda_{\mathfrak C}
 \le\left(2+\frac8{\log B}\right)\lceil B^t\rceil,
 \qquad
 \log\lambda_{\mathfrak C}=t\log B+O_B(1).
\end{equation}

It remains to estimate the full mass, including the dangling parts.
Given whole-rule crossing, the long branch crosses with probability $1/(1+p_c)$ by \eqref{eq:density-critical}.
On this event each block has its crossing-conditioned law.
In each of its paths, the first edge has conditional opening probability at least $p_c$, because block crossing is an increasing event.
Whenever this edge is open it is attached to the retained block terminal, so it contributes a connected child even if the rest of its path fails.
The connected diagonal entry of the full mass matrix therefore gives
\[
 \rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})\ge M_{c,c}
 \ge\frac{p_c}{1+p_c}\lceil B^t\rceil\lceil t(4/3)^t\rceil
 >\frac13\lceil B^t\rceil\lceil t(4/3)^t\rceil.
\]

For the upper bound, first examine the union of both terminal components of a block without conditioning.
On any length-$t$ path, its retained open edges lie in the two open prefixes from the path endpoints, whose expected total length is at most $2p_c/(1-p_c)<8$.
At most two closed frontier edges are also retained.
Hence a path contributes fewer than ten retained child cells on average.
Every globally retained child in a block lies in this local two-terminal union, since the block meets the rest of the rule only at its two terminals.
For each full parent state $c,b,u$, conditioning divides by $p_c$ or $1-p_c$, both greater than $1/5$.
The same bound applies to either inherited active-terminal choice for state $u$.
Each row sum of $\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C}$ is therefore less than
$50\lceil B^t\rceil\lceil t(4/3)^t\rceil+4$, including the two exterior edges and the short path.
A child in state $b$ is counted once, with both sides inherited from the same failed configuration.
The row-sum bound and the preceding lower bound yield
\begin{equation}\label{eq:density-mass-asymptotic}
 \frac13\lceil B^t\rceil\lceil t(4/3)^t\rceil
 <\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})
 <50\lceil B^t\rceil\lceil t(4/3)^t\rceil+4,
\end{equation}
and hence
$\log\rho(\mathbf M_{\mathfrak C})
=t(\log B+\log(4/3))+\log t+O(1)$.

For fixed $B$, Theorem~\ref{thm:heat-kernels} and these two logarithmic estimates show that the typical spectral dimensions of the constructed rules satisfy
\[
 \lim_{t\to\infty}\dim_{\mathrm S}^{(\mathrm N)}(\mathfrak C)
 =\frac{2(\log B+\log(4/3))}{2\log B+\log(4/3)}.
\]
Here $\mathfrak C$ is the critical cluster associated with the rule constructed at parameter $t$.
The expression on the right is continuous and strictly decreasing in $B>1$, with range $(1,2)$.
Given any nonempty open interval contained in $(1,2)$, choose a rational $B>1$ whose limiting value lies in that interval, and then choose a sufficiently large finite $t$.
The corresponding fixed classical rule has its typical spectral dimension in the prescribed interval, proving the theorem.
